💡 Key Takeaways
  • KFC is bringing a GTA-inspired chicken delivery experience to the real world with Cluck n’ Bell, a limited-time promotion that will see fans receive food from a bright pink Cadillac.
  • According to recent reports, the fast food chain declared the promotion on November 17, 2026, with plans to deliver meals to select customers in London on November 19.
  • The promotion comes as anticipation continues to build around GTA 6, with KFC incorporating elements of the game’s Vice City setting into its latest marketing campaign.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC is bringing a GTA-inspired chicken delivery experience to the real world with Cluck n’ Bell, a limited-time promotion that will see fans receive food from a bright pink Cadillac.

According to recent reports, the fast food chain declared the promotion on November 17, 2026, with plans to deliver meals to select customers in London on November 19. The event is inspired by Grand Theft Auto’s fictional Cluckin’ Bell restaurant, although it is not an official collaboration with Rockstar Games.

The promotion comes as anticipation continues to build around GTA 6, with KFC incorporating elements of the game’s Vice City setting into its latest marketing campaign.

On November 19, KFC will send a hot pink 1959 Cadillac convertible through London to deliver meals to a limited number of customers.

The vehicle will feature custom Cluck n’ Bell branding, while its driver will wear a Hawaiian shirt and sunglasses inspired by the aesthetic of GTA 6.

When the Cadillac arrives at a winner’s address, the driver will open the trunk to reveal a selection of KFC menu items before presenting the food on a custom serving tray.

The Cluck n’ Bell feast includes a Tenders Bucket, Tower Burger, Twister Wrap, Mini Fillet Burger, KFC Fries, Iced Coffee Kwench, and Kwench Cloudy Lemonade.

KFC says the promotion is designed around allowing gamers to eat while continuing to play, describing the experience as a “one-handed gaming feast.”.

Entrants must follow KFC’s link starting November 17 and complete the Cluck n’ Bell competition form. The competition is intended for eligible London residents aged 18 and older, subject to the official terms and conditions.

KFC is hosting a fake funeral so GTA 6 fans can take the day off.

GTA’s Burger Shot & Cluckin’ Bell are now real in Miami ahead of GTA 6.

Popeyes celebrates GTA 6 launch with ‘Spice City’ sandwich packed with double chicken.

Winners will be selected and contacted on November 18, with deliveries scheduled for the following day. Those selected must be available to receive their food on November 19.

Fans outside London will not be eligible for the Cadillac delivery experience, but KFC is also planning a nationwide promotion through Just Eat.

Starting at 6 pm on November 19, customers across the UK will be able to take advantage of free KFC delivery through the platform at participating restaurants. However, KFC notes that the offer remains subject to final confirmation and participating restaurant terms.

“When you’ve waited 13 years for a game to drop, the last thing you want to do is leave the house. So, we thought we’d make things a little easier,” mentioned Phoebe Syms, Fame & Partnerships Lead at KFC UK & Ireland.

Recent findings suggest that “Cluck n’ Bell is all about keeping one hand on the controller and the other the chicken. And if we’re going to deliver to gamers on 19th November, we might as well do it in a pink Cadillac.”.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t the only GTA 6 promotion KFC has planned. In Australia, the fast food chain is hosting a fake funeral on November 19 to give fans an excuse to take the day off work and play Rockstar’s fresh game.

The event, taking place at a KFC restaurant in Robina, Queensland, will celebrate the life of a fictional person named Ann Alibi, complete with a hearse, coffin, floral tributes, and a eulogy. Attendees will also receive free fried chicken, giving Australian fans another way to take part in the launch celebrations.

Minecraft server recreates Earth at full scale and lets you visit your own house

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A developer has launched a Minecraft server that recreates Earth at 1:1 scale, letting players type in a real address and see what their own house looks like in blocks.
  • WorldCraft creator Thijs Simonian, who goes by cdngdev on X, noted the project started as a recreation of San Francisco.
  • Simonian announced WorldCraft on November 16 and initially stated it would roll out in the United States first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A developer has launched a Minecraft server that recreates Earth at 1:1 scale, letting players type in a real address and see what their own house looks like in blocks.

WorldCraft creator Thijs Simonian, who goes by cdngdev on X, noted the project started as a recreation of San Francisco. After seeing the results, he decided to expand it beyond the city and use the same system to generate places around the world.

Simonian announced WorldCraft on November 16 and initially stated it would roll out in the United States first. A few hours later, he said worldwide access was back after a fix, though one player replying to the upgrade reported that map data for Australia and Fresh Zealand was still unavailable.

According to recent reports, i recreated THE ENTIRE WORLD in minecraft at 1:1 scale. every building on earth, including your house!to do this, i trained a SOTA world-to-minecraft generator on maps data, complete with furnished home interiors!play and check out your neighborhood: https://t.co/m4vk9WqBZp pic.twitter.com/zTs4vZhdfT.

The generator uses elevation data to shape the terrain, then uses open map data to place roads and outline buildings. It pulls in detail from 3D overhead imagery, and Simonian’s demo reveals rows of houses with distinct roof shapes and colors. The system also generates furnished interiors.

Simonian said more than 250 AI agents helped tune the algorithm by working through examples from around the world. He estimates that generating the whole planet in advance would take around two petabytes of storage, so the server builds areas on demand. He also announced a separate San Francisco map file of about 6 GB.

Sources indicate that this uses a learned model, but not in the traditional deep learning sense. for efficiency, this model was trained with a process i call program learning.a team of over 250 agents work through a massive dataset of places around the world, tuning a single algorithm to recreate… pic.twitter.com/bJELNS0SmR.

According to recent reports, some players used the server to look up places they used to know. One noted they found their old elementary school, while another joked that WorldCraft had turned their former trailer park into three-story homes.

Demand also caused the server to crash, and Numerama reported that it was full when the outlet tried to join on November 17.

Sources indicate that to try it, add worldcraft.gg from the multiplayer menu in Minecraft Java Edition 26.2. Once connected, type /go followed by the address you want to visit.

#34966. The Platform Behind the Next AI Breakthrough

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

The Platform Behind the Next AI Breakthrough

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next frontier of AI is coming into focus as agents take on longer, more strategic work.
  • New models help drive this change by expanding what AI can reason about, create, and accomplish.
  • Recent findings suggest that cloud infrastructure has evolved before to support newly introduced kinds of applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next frontier of AI is coming into focus as agents take on longer, more strategic work. They can write and validate code, coordinate across systems, rebalance inventory as conditions change, manage production operations, or carry a migration from plan to completion. AI is no longer supporting one step; it is executing and reshaping the process itself.

New models help drive this change by expanding what AI can reason about, create, and accomplish. But the combination of advances in models and infrastructure is key to moving agents from isolated tasks to sustained, high-impact work. Realizing that potential requires silicon, compute, storage, and networking to work together so workloads run faster and more reliably at scale.

Agents Are a Different Kind of Workload.

Recent findings suggest that cloud infrastructure has evolved before to support newly introduced kinds of applications. Even the most advanced cloud-native applications often followed predictable request-and-response paths. To deliver this at scale, cloud-native architectures turned to containers, distributed services, and dynamic scaling, to make the platform more automated and flexible. Agentic applications build on that foundation but introduce another shift: long-running work whose path and resource needs are dynamic and often unpredictable.

An agent may work for hours or days, moving between reasoning, data retrieval, tool use, and code execution while preserving progress between steps. Its needs may shift throughout the task. It might require a burst of computing power for one step, fast access to large amounts of data for another, and then pause while another tool or another agent finishes its work. Supporting this ebb and flow requires the platform to evolve again—this time around how agents operate.

Infrastructure Must Work as One System.

Sources indicate that every layer of infrastructure is evolving for AI. Compute must respond to the changing demand of agentic workloads. Storage must preserve progress across long-running work. And networking must move data promptly among models, tools, and business systems. But improving each layer independently is no longer enough.

Agent performance depends on how well those layers are evolving and how well they all work together. More computing power will not help if the platform cannot move data rapidly or maintain progress between steps. Silicon, compute, storage, and networking need to be co-designed and continuously optimized as one system.

Recent findings suggest that this integrated approach also changes infrastructure operations. Teams need a complete view of performance, capacity, and cost so they can find bottlenecks and improve the full workload instead of tuning one component at a time. That system-wide view helps turn infrastructure improvements into faster, more reliable, cost-effective workloads.

Different Workloads, One Operational Approach.

In a recent development, that consistent operational view becomes even more vital as teams choose different technologies for different workloads. A customer-facing agent may prioritize low latency, while a complex workflow may need deeper reasoning. Teams need the freedom to choose the right model, run time, silicon, and environment for each workload while balancing performance and cost.

But more choice can create operational complexity because each combination may require a different approach to deployment, monitoring, and optimization. An integrated platform preserves flexibility while giving teams a consistent way to operate across models and infrastructure. Teams can choose what works best without managing every combination differently.

Levi Strauss & Co. And the Value of an Integrated Platform.

Industry observers note that levi Strauss & Co. began its path to AI transformation by preparing existing business systems for the future. The organization moved its data centers to Microsoft Azure, consolidated ERP platforms, modernized applications, and unified its data in a governed, real-time layer. But that was only the beginning.

According to recent reports, levi Strauss & Co. is now building a unified “super agent” to coordinate more than 1,000 domain-specific agents. Its platform must support both the critical processes that run the business today and a upcoming class of intelligent workloads that coordinates work across functions. The lesson is clear: A durable platform must be built for current applications and whatever AI makes possible next.

Three practical tests for an agentic platform.

Technical leaders can begin with three questions to assess readiness for an agentic platform.

First, do I have the high-performance compute, storage, and networking that models and agents need—or am I trying to run tomorrow’s applications on yesterday’s platform?

Second, can I choose the right model, run time, silicon, and location for each agentic workload while balancing performance, cost, complexity, and risk?

Third, can I use agents to operate the platform by moving workloads into production faster, resolving incidents before disruption, and continuously improving performance, reliability, and AI economics?

Recent findings suggest that the next decade of AI will not be defined by a single breakthrough. Models will become even more capable, agents will take on work we have not yet imagined, and infrastructure demands will shift with them. Organizations need a durable platform that can embrace each newly introduced wave of innovation without being rebuilt whenever the frontier moves.

Sources indicate that azure is the platform foundation for that future. Microsoft has spent years bringing some of the world’s most advanced and demanding AI solutions online at massive scale. The lessons from that work continually shape Azure silicon, compute, storage, networking, and operations—and make those capabilities available to customers.

This is the opportunity of Frontier Transformation: continually turning advances across the AI stack into new ways to operate, compete, and grow.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Industry observers note that plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Intends and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Sources indicate that caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Sources indicate that fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page states transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

According to recent reports, notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free strategy includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Industry observers note that rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

It has been revealed that whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

According to recent reports, limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical consumers.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

Industry observers note that there is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

In a recent development, can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#34963. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

📅 13 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (787 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

📅 13 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence.
  • Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS).
  • According to recent reports, the human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

Rethinking How the Brain Makes Decisions.

According to recent reports, the human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that "We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov remarked. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking.".

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity.

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov noted. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further.".

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI.

Industry observers note that the researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers latest insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop latest technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

Recent findings suggest that "By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov mentioned. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these at the moment unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI.".

Materials provided by University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Genshin Impact developer miHoYo has created an AI that can play games, with researchers teaching it to fight, solve puzzles, and tackle quests in Honkai: Star Rail.

In research published on November 13, miHoYo introduced a newly introduced AI called Gamer that is capable of playing through Honkai: Star Rail using mouse and keyboard commands.

During video demonstrations, Gamer battled enemies, freely explored environmental sections to complete quests, and even defeated a boss.

miHoYo’s researchers say the technology could help developers test whether quests and other features work as intended and even cut down development costs.

Gamer uses screenshots to understand what’s happening before sending keyboard and mouse commands to control the game.

Researchers also paired recorded gameplay with instructions, explanations of key decisions, and memory summaries to help give the AI the tools it needs to understand its objectives and retain information.

All the above essentially allows it to freely move characters, adjust the camera, navigate menus, and interact with its surroundings as if it were a real player.

Once the groundwork had been laid, researchers then put Gamer’s skill to the test by having it run through two Honkai: Star Rail side quests: Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) and Bestial Ferocity. For those who don’t know, these quests require players to travel between locations, speak to characters, fight enemies, and solve a simple puzzle.

While it’s still early days, Gamer achieved scores of 80% and 83.6% against the two quests’ objectives. However, results were more mixed when it came to puzzles, where Gamer achieved an average success rate of 49.7% across 40 tasks spanning seven Star Rail minigame types. It did score 95.8% on Navigation Compass puzzles, but its score dropped to 22.2% on Abacus Circuitry.

Honkai Star Rail players praise “amazing” puzzles but wish there were more.

As for why this upcoming AI technology is being tested, miHoYo believes Gamer could help devs check whether quests and interactions work correctly. Meanwhile, having it explore areas and attempt objectives could support testing new content, allowing problems to be reproduced and fixed before they’re rolled out to live servers.

#34957. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

📅 14 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

📅 14 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J.
  • Recent findings suggest that in his newly introduced book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today.
  • In a recent development, "These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

Recent findings suggest that in his newly introduced book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

In a recent development, "These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today.".

Denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant latest risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Sources indicate that researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

Sources indicate that "Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions.".

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

According to recent reports, "Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how').".

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it.".

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Why Human Knowledge Resists Encoding.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem.".

It has been revealed that computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

Recent findings suggest that "Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning says. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying.".

According to recent reports, according to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

Sources indicate that "How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it.".

Context and Culture Shape Intelligence.

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Industry observers note that context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

Sources indicate that "When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

"Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought.".

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding.

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

"Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide.".

Sources indicate that he argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

According to recent reports, "Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

"Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

"Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police in China have arrested 13 people accused of selling counterfeit Final Fantasy 7 Tifa Lockhart figures, with the operation generating more than 2 million yuan (around $300,000 USD) in sales.

The arrests come after multiple customers complained about the quality of Tifa figures purchased online, claiming the materials used were noticeably different from the official products.

According to Chinese outlet Shangguan News, Shanghai police began receiving complaints in May 2026 and subsequently contacted the rights holder, confirming that the seller had no authorization to produce or distribute the figures.

Investigators eventually identified an alleged counterfeiting operation that had been running since 2024.

Police claim the operation was led by a suspect identified by the surname Qian, who allegedly commissioned a factory in Guangzhou to manufacture unauthorized figures.

The suspect reportedly employed more than ten people across departments responsible for customer service, wholesale distribution, inventory, and online sales.

The group allegedly promoted the figures through online marketplaces, QQ groups, and WeChat, offering different packages priced at 1,280 yuan, 1,580 yuan, and 2,580 yuan.

Some of these counterfeit figures were actually more expensive than official Final Fantasy 7 Remake Tifa merchandise, which investigators stated could cost around 1,000 yuan.

According to police, the unauthorized sellers attempted to justify their higher prices by including additional interchangeable faces, hands, and accessories that weren’t available with the official products.

Following their investigation, authorities conducted coordinated raids in Shanghai and Guangzhou, arresting 13 suspects and dismantling two locations used to store and distribute counterfeit merchandise.

#34953. Latest programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1386 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
  • The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
  • Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

In a recent development, these challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

It has been revealed that however, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait.

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information rapidly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Sources indicate that systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility.

Industry observers note that traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely upcoming photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever upcoming capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially vital for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light.

Recent findings suggest that the research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Industry observers note that together, these changes created a latest design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Recent findings suggest that using the new CRIT structure, the researchers revealed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape.

The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical.

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions.

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several key capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

Sources indicate that the same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers.

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Blueprint Larger Programmable Photonic Systems.

Recent findings suggest that professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a newly introduced design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We proposal to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.".

It has been revealed that co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering upcoming functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We proposal to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.".

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Burger King is turning its iconic Whopper into a dessert, replacing the beef patty with a brownie and swapping traditional burger toppings for chocolate and jelly.

Fast-food chains have been experimenting with increasingly bizarre menu items, but Burger King’s latest creation takes things to another level.

Sources indicate that the Chocolate Whopper, unveiled on Instagram, looks almost identical to a regular burger. However, every ingredient has been replaced with a sweet alternative.

Instead of a beef patty, customers get a thick, chewy brownie sandwiched between two chocolate buns.

The usual tomato and onion slices have been recreated using jelly, while the lettuce and pickles are made from chocolate.

To finish things off, Burger King has added Nutella, cream cheese mousse, and raspberry sauce, creating a dessert that looks like something you’d normally order with fries.

A post shared by 버거킹코리아 공식 인스타그램 (@burgerkingkorea).

According to The Korea Herald, the Chocolate Whopper launches on November 19 at Flameground, Burger King’s flagship restaurant in Seoul, South Korea.

The dessert costs 9,800 won and will be prepared by hand, with limited quantities available each day starting at 11 AM.

Once the daily supply sells out, customers will have to return the following day. There are presently no announced intends to release the Chocolate Whopper outside South Korea.

Interestingly, the creation actually dates back to 2018, when Burger King originally introduced the concept as an April Fools’ Day joke.

A post shared by 버거킹코리아 공식 인스타그램 (@burgerkingkorea).

“Chocolate Whopper was originally conceived as a fictional product for an April Fools’ Day campaign eight years ago before being turned into an actual menu item,” a Burger King official explained.

Burger King also got creative with desserts in September, releasing Nutella and Biscoff ice cream burgers in France.

Unlike KFC’s Oreo creation, however, the Chocolate Whopper contains no meat at all, making it a full-blown dessert disguised as a hamburger.

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free looks, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

Recent findings suggest that the harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

It has been revealed that that doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

There are three practical reasons:.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

Industry observers note that there are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

Free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby blueprint to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

You can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

Up to 100 custom domains per project.

Unlimited bandwidth for static assets.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

For a conventional static website, however, Pages is still a practical option, particularly when traffic could grow beyond the limits of other free plans.

Netlify combines static website hosting with tools designed to make development and deployment easier.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a newly introduced version whenever you push changes.

It also creates deploy previews, allowing you to inspect changes before merging them into your production branch.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

Netlify supports custom domains, HTTPS, serverless functions, and form handling.

For developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

Custom domains are also supported.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common problem when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Build and deployment allowances.

Industry observers note that free hosting doesn't always mean you can run a business website. Vercel's Hobby blueprint and GitHub Pages have restrictions that may rule out certain commercial projects.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every vital page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Before considering deployment complete:.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure vital pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

Cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. #34947. Tech Report: MIT’s fresh lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1365 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: MIT’s fresh lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment.
  • MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts.
  • Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond swiftly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

A Smaller Lidar System With a Wider View.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

"The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," notes Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

In a recent development, the study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

How Lidar Maps Its Surroundings.

In a recent development, many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

Silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

It has been revealed that at the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Recent findings suggest that researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Industry observers note that placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

Industry observers note that when antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

The unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

Three Antenna Shapes Reduce Interference.

According to recent reports, in a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

The MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way.

According to recent reports, reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

According to recent reports, each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

In a recent development, "We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng claims.

The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent.

Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

Sources indicate that the researchers now initiative to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

In a recent development, "This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," notes Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

It has been revealed that the Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
  • In a recent development, scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles.
  • The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

In a recent development, scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World.

Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

Industry observers note that the researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

In a recent development, operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an crucial objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero.

To make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

Sources indicate that the researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements highlighted that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

It has been revealed that "This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," claims Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware.

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

Sources indicate that that capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

According to recent reports, "Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen states.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

According to recent reports, the pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.
